story.headline: US and Saudi strikes hit Iraq militias
story.summary: Joint US-Saudi air strikes killed at least 20 Iran-backed PMF fighters across Iraq, the first major US military action since Trump paused the Iran bombing campaign.
story.display_body: US and Saudi Arabia carried out joint air strikes on Iran-backed militias in Iraq before dawn on Wednesday 29 July, the first major US military action in the Middle East since President Trump paused a 13-day bombing campaign last Friday (24 July). Iraq's Popular Mobilisation Forces (PMF — an umbrella of Iraqi militias trained and backed by Iran, and legally part of Iraq's own security apparatus) said at least 20 of its members were killed and 32 wounded in strikes across several sites. Saudi Arabia and US Central Command (CENTCOM) said the operation targeted militias responsible for drone attacks on American troops and on Saudi oil facilities in the Eastern Province and around Riyadh; Riyadh said it "does not seek escalation" but would respond to aggression. The PMF called the strikes a "highly dangerous escalation" and a violation of Iraqi sovereignty, while the Islamic Resistance in Iraq denied any role in the attacks on Saudi Arabia and called the kingdom's claims "fabrications" — so responsibility for the drone attacks that Riyadh cites as justification is itself contested. Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi convened an emergency national-security council meeting and is expected to travel to Saudi Arabia on Thursday 30 July.
story.why: It pulls the Iraqi state into a fight between its own Iran-aligned forces and the US-Saudi axis just days into a fragile pause in the wider Iran war, and risks reigniting a conflict Washington had declared suspended.

story.headline: Kumamoto quake death toll rises to 13
story.summary: The death toll from the magnitude-7.1 earthquake in Kumamoto Prefecture, Japan, rose to at least 13 with five more feared dead as rescuers searched a collapsed shopping mall.
story.display_body: The death toll from the magnitude-7.1 earthquake that struck Kumamoto Prefecture on the Japanese island of Kyushu rose to at least 13 confirmed dead on Wednesday 29 July, with five more feared dead and rescuers still searching a collapsed shopping mall. The quake hit Tuesday 28 July at 16:27 local time (07:27 GMT); the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA) put it at magnitude 7.1 while the US Geological Survey measured 6.8. At least three of the deaths came at an Aeon shopping mall in the town of Kashima, where a gas explosion after the tremor tore through the building and collapsed a large section, the retailer's president confirmed. A wall of the centuries-old Kumamoto Castle also partly collapsed, and Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi said the toll was expected to rise as police, firefighters and Self-Defense Forces personnel continued the search.
story.why: It is the deadliest quake to hit Kyushu since the 2016 Kumamoto disaster, and the death toll has climbed sharply from the "at least 50 injured" reported when the tremor first struck.

story.headline: Senate advances Russia sanctions bill
story.summary: The US Senate voted 86-12 to advance a Russia sanctions bill renamed for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, a procedural step that authorizes but does not yet impose sweeping tariffs on Russian imports.
story.display_body: The US Senate voted 86-12 on Tuesday 28 July to advance a Russia sanctions bill, a bipartisan procedural step that its sponsors described as largely symbolic ahead of the chamber's August recess. The measure, renamed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia Act of 2026 after the South Carolina senator who died suddenly of an aortic tear, would give the president new authority to sanction Russian officials, foreign nationals and financial institutions tied to Moscow's war effort, compel a 500% tariff on all Russian imports including oil and gas, and expand powers to punish "shadow fleet" vessels evading energy sanctions. Only one Republican, Rand Paul, joined 11 Democrats against it; Graham's sister Darline, appointed to fill his seat, is a lead sponsor. The Senate will need several more votes for the bill to pass, and the House passed its own version in June.
story.why: The lopsided vote signals durable cross-party support for tougher Russia measures, but Tuesday's step authorizes rather than imposes the tariffs — the sanctions are not yet law.

story.headline: Keiko Fujimori sworn in as Peru president
story.summary: Keiko Fujimori was inaugurated as Peru's president for 2026-2031, becoming the country's ninth head of state in a decade and vowing a hardline crackdown on crime.
story.display_body: Keiko Fujimori was sworn in as Peru's president on Tuesday 28 July for the 2026-2031 term, becoming the country's ninth head of state in a decade and vowing a hardline crackdown on crime. Fujimori, 51, daughter of the late former president Alberto Fujimori (in office 1990-2000, imprisoned for corruption and crimes against humanity), won the 7 June runoff by fewer than 50,000 votes over leftist rival Roberto Sanchez, after losing three previous runoffs. She pledged to deploy the military for "order" in areas hit by gangs, drug trafficking and illegal mining, and floated mass deportation of irregular migrants, anonymous judges, and prison labour in exchange for food. Homicides in Peru rose from about 1,000 in 2018 to 2,600 in 2025, and extortion complaints jumped from 3,200 to 26,500 over the same period.
story.why: Her inauguration marks the return of "fujimorismo" to power in a country worn down by chronic political instability and its worst security crisis in decades.

story.headline: UBS Q2 net profit rises 17 percent
story.summary: UBS reported second-quarter net profit up 17% to $2.8 billion, with the Credit Suisse integration on track to largely finish by year-end.
story.display_body: UBS reported second-quarter net profit up 17% to $2.8 billion (CHF 2.3 billion) on Wednesday 29 July, with pre-tax operating profit jumping 64% to $3.59 billion. The results, under CEO Sergio Ermotti, come as the bank presses ahead with absorbing Credit Suisse, an integration it expects to largely complete by year-end. The rebound in profitability follows a period dominated by the costs and complexity of the 2023 emergency takeover of its former rival.
story.why: UBS is now Switzerland's only globally systemic bank, and its earnings trajectory feeds directly into the politically charged debate in Bern over how much additional capital the enlarged bank should be forced to hold.

story.headline: Zug funds research on system it pays into
story.summary: Canton Zug, the largest net contributor to Switzerland's fiscal equalization scheme, is helping fund a research centre that critically examines that same system, raising conflict-of-interest concerns.
story.display_body: The canton of Zug — by far the largest net contributor to Switzerland's inter-cantonal fiscal equalization system (the Finanzausgleich, which redistributes money from wealthy cantons to poorer ones) — is helping fund a new research centre that will critically examine that very system, SRF reported on Wednesday 29 July. Zug's payments into the scheme have climbed to nearly CHF 500 million, and it will contribute several million francs toward building the centre. Lausanne economist Marius Bruelhart welcomed private funding of research in principle but warned the output must be clearly labelled as commissioned work, arguing Zug plainly has expectations about the findings and that genuinely independent research would have been put out to open tender.
story.why: It puts a spotlight on the conflict of interest when the biggest payer into a redistribution system bankrolls the scholarship used to argue for reforming it.

story.headline: Four win 2026 Fields Medals
story.summary: The IMU awarded the 2026 Fields Medals to Hong Wang, Yu Deng, John Pardon and Jacob Tsimerman at ICM Philadelphia.
story.display_body: At the opening ceremony of the International Congress of Mathematicians in Philadelphia on Thursday 23 July, the International Mathematical Union awarded the 2026 Fields Medals — the discipline's most prestigious prize, given every four years to mathematicians under 40 — to four researchers. Hong Wang (New York University; Institut des Hautes Études Scientifiques) was cited for work in geometric measure theory, including her proof (with Joshua Zahl) of the three-dimensional Kakeya conjecture — roughly, that a set able to contain a unit line segment pointing in every direction cannot be thin, a question open for decades that underpins deep problems in analysis. She is only the third woman to win in the medal's 90-year history. Yu Deng (University of Chicago) was honoured for partial-differential-equations work including a rigorous derivation of the Boltzmann equation — the master equation of gas kinetics — from colliding hard spheres, progress on one of David Hilbert's 1900 problems. John Pardon (Stony Brook University) was recognised for symplectic geometry and topology, and Jacob Tsimerman (University of Toronto) for number theory and the geometry underlying it. The IMU also gave the Abacus Medal (for theoretical computer science) to Shayan Oveis Gharan of the University of Washington, the Chern Medal to Graeme Segal, the Gauss Prize to Yurii Nesterov, and the Leelavati public-outreach prize to Hannah Fry.
story.why: The Fields citations are a four-yearly snapshot of which mathematical problems the field judges most consequential — this year, questions where pure mathematics meets the foundations of physics and computation.

story.headline: Muon g-2 puzzle shifts to the colliders
story.summary: Lattice QCD now matches the measured muon g-2, but a CMD-3 pion-production discrepancy leaves the data-driven method clashing with other colliders.
story.display_body: For 25 years the muon — a heavy cousin of the electron — has been physics' most tantalising anomaly: its magnetic wobble in a field (measured as g-2, the tiny excess over the naïve value of 2) came out larger than the Standard Model seemed to predict, hinting at undiscovered particles. This Quanta feature lays out how that story inverted. The hardest part of the prediction is the strong nuclear force's contribution. Two methods exist: the data-driven approach infers it from measured electron-positron collision rates, and lattice QCD (quantum chromodynamics simulated on a spacetime grid) computes it from first principles. In 2021 the BMW collaboration's lattice result matched Fermilab's precise measurement almost exactly — and independent lattice groups have since agreed — suggesting the muon behaves exactly as known physics requires, with no new particles needed. The puzzle now is why the older data-driven prediction disagrees. The prime suspect: the CMD-3 detector at the VEPP-2000 collider in Novosibirsk, whose 2023 measurement of the pion-pair production cross section (a proxy for the strong-force contribution) came out significantly higher than every previous experiment, clashing with results from other colliders. Physicists are still trying to determine whether this is an experimental artefact or a genuine sign that something is off.
story.why: A 5-sigma discovery that quietly dissolved into a disagreement between experiments is a cautionary tale about how a headline anomaly's fate can hinge on an unglamorous cross-section measurement — and the muon verdict is not yet final.

story.headline: First stars may light an early gas clump
story.summary: A model finds a Population III star cluster fits JWST data on the He II emitter Hebe better than an accreting black hole.
story.display_body: Hebe is a blob of gas seen by JWST just 450 million years after the Big Bang, next to the luminous galaxy GN-z11. It glows with a distinctive helium-II emission line, which needs a source of very energetic ultraviolet light. Two candidates can supply that: a cluster of Population III stars (the universe's hypothetical first generation, made of pristine hydrogen and helium with no heavier elements, and never yet confirmed) or an accreting supermassive black hole. Jeon and colleagues modelled both against JWST's several measured line fluxes at once. An accreting black hole could match any single flux with plausible parameters, but struggled to fit all the measurements simultaneously; a Pop III cluster of a few hundred thousand solar masses gave the best joint fit. The authors are careful about scope: this is a modelling argument, not a detection, and they note the two explanations are not mutually exclusive — Hebe could host both.
story.why: Confirming the first stars is one of the marquee goals of the JWST era; Hebe is a concrete candidate where the first-stars reading now has the quantitative edge, though it is far from settled.

story.headline: Two drugs cut long-COVID risk in trials
story.summary: Randomized placebo-controlled trials show metformin and nirmatrelvir (Paxlovid) each reduce the risk of long COVID after infection.
story.display_body: Observational data had long hinted that the diabetes drug metformin and the antiviral Paxlovid (nirmatrelvir-ritonavir) might blunt long COVID, but rigorous randomized, placebo-controlled evidence was missing. That gap is now closing. In the ACTIV-6 platform trial, 2,983 outpatient adults aged 30 and over with acute SARS-CoV-2 were randomized to a 14-day course of metformin or placebo within 7 days of symptom onset; metformin roughly halved the rate of clinician-diagnosed long COVID at six months (a secondary outcome). Separately, Nature reports that a randomized trial of Paxlovid in 144 people cut the three-month risk of long COVID by about 40% versus placebo, published 16 July in The Lancet Infectious Diseases; I could not independently open that primary, so those figures rest on Nature's account. Both are repurposed, widely available medicines, and the effects are relative risk reductions in modest-to-large samples, not cures.
story.why: Long COVID has had almost no proven prevention; two cheap, familiar drugs showing benefit in controlled trials is the first real foothold — but the metformin benefit was a secondary endpoint and the Paxlovid trial is small, so both need confirmation before they become standard advice.
